Daniel’s “listen to your heart” framing smuggles in a major assumption: that the “heart” one is listening to is already *cultivated* rather than merely *felt*. His own story makes that clear—ten years of deliberate self-scrutiny effectively trained an inner conscience until it aligned with explicit moral rules. That is closer to reflective equilibrium (testing intuitions against principles and revising both) than to spontaneity, and it sits in a long lineage: Hume and Adam Smith treat moral judgment as sentiment, but specifically *educated* sentiment shaped by perspective-taking and social feedback ([*The Theory of Moral Sentiments*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Moral_Sentiments)). Put differently, Daniel’s “heart” is not raw emotion; it’s a practiced instrument. Without that distinction, “follow your emotional truths” risks becoming advice to obey whichever intuition happens to win today—exactly the problem social psychology has repeatedly highlighted in work on motivated reasoning and post-hoc moral justification (e.g., Haidt’s intuition-first model in [*The Righteous Mind*](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/202430/the-righteous-mind-by-jonathan-haidt/)).

The more interesting (and underdeveloped) point is his title: “privilege.” The privilege here is not just personal weirdness; it’s access to the prerequisites that make moral self-cultivation feasible—time, psychological safety, exposure to critique, and communities that reward honesty over status-protection. If Daniel wants the view to travel, he may need to translate “listen to your heart” into *train your heart* (and specify training conditions): what kinds of practices produced this alignment, what guardrails prevented self-criticism from turning into rumination or self-harm, and what external checks kept the “heart” from simply internalizing local biases. Without those missing pieces, the blog’s admirable humility (“a lot” may be untrue) reads less like a concession and more like the central lesson: moral intuition is always case-bound, socially shaped, and only sometimes trustworthy—usually after disciplined work that many people, for structural reasons, cannot easily do.
